summary: Describes how to specify holes in geodetic service boundaries for Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) and one way of searching a service database to handle them. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A region on a map with a cut-out where a different service applies, plus how to look up the right one.

questions: what is a lost service boundary hole
how are holes specified in gml polygons
how does a lost server pick between overlapping areas
subtitle: Rules for cutting holes in the map areas that decide which emergency or other service a location maps to.

tldr.problem: A LoST service area can contain exception areas that must map to a different destination, and unconstrained polygon encodings are hard to process.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5964 profiles GML polygons with three rules for holes, written as interior boundaries, and describes a lookup that checks the exterior boundary and then the holes.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can stay simple and still interoperate, and LoST servers can answer location queries quickly.

facts.label: Hole intersections
facts.value: At most one point between two holes

today: RFC 5964 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Holes in Service Boundaries
sections.content:
The LoST protocol (RFC 5222) maps a service and a location to destination addresses. A LoST server does this by provisioning boundary maps against service URNs. Each boundary is a polygon of geodetic coordinates, called the exterior polygon. Sometimes it contains exception areas, or holes, that for the same service must yield a different destination.

RFC 5964 describes a profile of Geographic Markup Language (GML) polygons that removes permutations that are difficult to process. This allows simpler implementations, and a fully conformant GML implementation must produce polygons that fit the profile.

The working group noted that such regions could be drawn as polygons without holes, but chose these recommendations to avoid problems with arbitrary division of regions and to align with existing geospatial practice.
sections.eli5: A big area has a smaller patch inside where the rules differ. This document says how to describe that patch so every computer reads it the same way.

sections.title: The Three Rules for Holes
sections.content:
Rule 1: two holes MUST NOT have more than one point of intersection. If holes overlap or share a common boundary, they represent a single hole, so common boundaries are removed and one hole is created.

Rule 2: a polygon MUST describe a contiguous region. A hole that overlaps the outer boundary or shares part of a side with it has an inlet, and the region MUST be expressed without the hole. If a hole touches the outer boundary in two places, the region MUST be expressed as two separate polygons. A polygon entirely inside a hole, an island, is likewise a separate polygon.

Rule 3: a hole MUST be a legal linear ring in accordance with the geoshape specification, except that its points go clockwise. The exterior boundary goes counterclockwise, so the upward normals oppose each other. The number of points is not restricted.
sections.eli5: Holes that touch merge into one. A hole cannot reach the edge or split the shape. You draw holes in the opposite direction to the outline.

sections.title: Holes in GML
sections.content:
A GML polygon has an enclosed exterior boundary whose first and last points are the same. Vertices can be written with <pos> elements or a <posList> element.

A hole is an interior boundary inside the polygon. In the RFC's example, a hexagon with exterior points A to F gets an interior <gml:interior> ring of four points, w, x, y and z, and the area those points enclose is the hole.
sections.eli5: The outline is listed first, then a second list of points draws the cut-out inside it.

sections.title: Boundaries and Selection
sections.content:
A service boundary's enclosed area is where a service URN maps to a single URI. The RFC's example has two boundaries: area-A, the hexagon with a hole, and area-w, the hole itself. Since area-w is also a service boundary, it needs its own separate polygon, with the vertices reversed. In the LoST mappings, area-A is "Outer Area Police" and area-w is "Inner Area Police", both for urn:service:sos.police.

Each polygon is stored in a geospatial database mapped to a service URN and destination URI. Many such databases support interior exclusions natively. Without that, interior boundaries can be stored with the polygon and checked separately. A location falls inside a polygon if it is within the exterior boundary and not within any interior boundary. So a location in the hole maps to Inner Area Police, and one in the hexagon but outside the hole maps to Outer Area Police.

The RFC considers it likely that LoST servers must respond fast enough for real-time queries in an emergency call routing flow, which is why native geospatial queries and easily mapped boundaries are preferred.
sections.eli5: To find the right helper, check whether the spot is in the big area and not in any cut-out. If it is in a cut-out, ask that area's helper instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that constraining the polygon representation does not introduce new security considerations.
sections.eli5: Setting tidier drawing rules does not create any new dangers.

data.title: Polygon with a hole (abridged)
data.code:
<gml:Polygon srsName="urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326">
  <gml:exterior>
    <gml:LinearRing>
      <gml:pos>43.311 -73.422</gml:pos> <!--A-->
      ... B, C, D, E, F ...
      <gml:pos>43.311 -73.422</gml:pos> <!--A-->
    </gml:LinearRing>
  </gml:exterior>
  <gml:interior>
    <gml:LinearRing>
      <gml:pos>43.411 -73.322</gml:pos> <!--w-->
      <gml:pos>43.411 -73.222</gml:pos> <!--x-->
      <gml:pos>43.211 -73.222</gml:pos> <!--y-->
      <gml:pos>43.211 -73.322</gml:pos> <!--z-->
      <gml:pos>43.411 -73.322</gml:pos> <!--w-->
    </gml:LinearRing>
  </gml:interior>
</gml:Polygon>
